titre: The Lieber Code (1863): A Military Order Turned Model
accroche: On April 24, 1863, Lincoln promulgates 157 articles drafted by a professor for the Union army alone. International codifications will draw on them.
contenu_vulgarise:
On April 24, 1863, in the middle of the Civil War, the Union army receives a text of 157 articles divided into ten sections: the Instructions for the Government of Armies of the United States in the Field, published as General Orders No. 100 and promulgated by President Lincoln. Its author is not a general. He is Francis Lieber, a professor at Columbia College who came from Germany at twenty-eight, and who wrote the text with a committee of four generals. It is not a treaty: it is an internal regulation, binding only on that army.

## A necessity that permits and that limits

It is often presented as a humanitarian charter. It begins instead with necessity. Article 14 defines it as the set of measures indispensable for securing the ends of the war and lawful according to the modern law and usages of war. Article 15 allows the direct destruction of the lives of armed enemies, the capture of every armed enemy, and the destruction of property and lines of communication. Article 17 goes further: it is lawful to starve the enemy belligerent, armed or unarmed, if that hastens his submission.

Yet the same text sets limits that an army's regulations were not used to writing. Article 16 says that military necessity does not admit of cruelty, that is, the infliction of suffering for the sake of suffering or for revenge, nor of maiming or wounding except in fighting, nor of torture to extort confessions. It does not admit of poison, nor of the wanton devastation of a district, and it does not include acts that make the return to peace unnecessarily difficult. Article 22 notes that the distinction between the private individual of a hostile country and the hostile state has been asserted over the centuries, and that the unarmed citizen is to be spared in person, property and honor as much as the exigencies of war will admit. Article 148 refuses to put a man outside the law, and treats rewards offered for assassinating an enemy as a return to barbarism.

Article 58 bears the mark of its time: the law of nations knows no distinction of color, and if an enemy enslaves captured soldiers, the response will be death, never enslavement. According to Wikipedia, it was written at a time when the Confederacy refused prisoner-of-war status to Black Union soldiers.

## The shift

The text has no force outside the Northern army, and yet it circulates. According to the Library of Congress, Prussia translates it and approves it for the war of 1870. It serves as the basis for the Brussels Declaration of 1874, itself the starting point of the Hague Conventions of 1899 and 1907. The Netherlands in 1871, France in 1877 and the United Kingdom in 1884 in turn publish manuals of the same kind.

What gets exported is a rule written by a belligerent for its own soldiers, which accepts necessity instead of fighting it. One can see in this a reason for its success, one that a limit imposed from outside would not have had: that is a reading, which the cited sources do not settle. Article 16 puts it its own way: necessity includes no act that makes the return to peace unnecessarily difficult.

repere.texte: The Instructions for the Government of Armies of the United States in the Field, drafted by Francis Lieber, comprise 157 articles in ten sections. They are promulgated by Lincoln on April 24, 1863 as General Orders No. 100.
repere.source: Yale Law School, Avalon Project, Instructions for the Government of Armies of the United States in the Field (General Orders No. 100, 1863)

carte.punch: The text that allows starving the enemy also bans torture: the Lieber Code, 1863.
carte.idee: In 1863, a Columbia professor drafts for the Union army 157 articles that accept military necessity and set bounds on it (no torture, no poison). This internal regulation inspires the Brussels Declaration of 1874, then The Hague.

quiz.question: Why can the Lieber Code both permit starving the enemy and forbid torture?
choix: Because it admits what is indispensable to end the war and lawful under its usages, and refuses suffering that serves no such end
Because the article on starvation covers only soldiers, and the one on torture only civilians
Because the article on starvation applies only to besieged places
Because the article on starvation was withdrawn before the text was promulgated
quiz.explication: Article 17 covers the enemy belligerent, armed or unarmed, so not only soldiers, and it does appear in the promulgated text. Article 17 is not limited to besieged places, and the code is an internal order of the Union army, not a treaty. The logic is that of military necessity (Articles 14 to 16): what is indispensable to end the war is permitted, what serves only to cause suffering is forbidden.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Does the Lieber Code directly inspire the Hague Conventions, or does it go through a relay?
choix: It directly inspires the Hague Conventions of 1899 and 1907, with no intermediate text
It serves as the basis for the Brussels Declaration of 1874, itself the starting point of The Hague
It had no influence outside the United States
It is first translated into French before reaching Prussia and then The Hague
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text serves as the basis for the Brussels Declaration of 1874, which is itself the starting point of the Hague Conventions of 1899 and 1907: there is a relay, not a direct link. It does, on the contrary, have influence outside the United States, with Prussia translating it for the war of 1870, and nothing in the sources says it reaches Prussia through French.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does Article 58 of the Lieber Code provide regarding an enemy who would enslave prisoners?
choix: The response will be death, never enslavement in return
The response will be the enslavement of enemy prisoners, in kind
The Union army must immediately free all its own prisoners
The code provides no response, to avoid escalation
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Article 58 says that the law of nations knows no distinction of color, and that if an enemy enslaves captured soldiers, the response will be death, never enslavement in return. The text provides neither a symmetrical enslavement, nor a unilateral release of Union prisoners, nor the absence of a response.
